name: Hamza Akhtar
backstory: Each year he buys one bunch of supermarket tulips and sets them on the kitchen windowsill, on a date no one else in the house knows is significant. He doesn't explain it to his partner or the child, and he would rather they didn't ask. His working life runs on exactness: dates, document numbers, who said what in which committee room, and he will not print a line he can't source. The exam that got him his first proper post, though, he cheated in, copying answers onto a strip of paper kept in his sleeve, and he has never told anyone. He wants to be safe and keeps his days narrow enough that little can reach him, but the one thing that ever improved his reporting was being wrong in public and having to stand there and say so.
persona: He spends weekends pulling council planning minutes and will correct a colleague's figure across the desk without softening it. He turned down the editor's job that would have moved him off the story, skips leaving drinks, and expects the council to let him down again, so it rarely catches him out. He trusts the people he lives with until they give him a reason not to, and he is content alone in the house, with the hallway lamp left low for whoever is coming home late. Neighbours find him precise and a little cold. After a picnic he gathers up every stray crumb before anyone else has stood up.
speaking_style: He speaks at an even, deliberate pace in full sentences. Dates and figures come out exactly as he would print them, so a rough number never survives him. He will stop a conversation to fix a loose word, and he closes a point with "that's what the record says."
mannerisms: describes a song, film or letter that moved them and asks if others felt it too
answers jokes with a brief dry line and no more

past.content: The boys on the back seat of the bus started calling me after a cartoon dog, and every morning I held my bag on my knees so they couldn't tip out my packed lunch.
Under a bench by the bus shelter there was a carrier bag stuffed with notes, and I walked it to the police station myself before I let myself think about it.
On the CV I typed a diploma I never finished, and I read the line three times before I sent it anyway.
Four months on the picket line outside the print works, standing there at six each morning with a flask of tea that was cold before the first van came.
I told my closest friend about the council contract I was chasing, and two weeks later the story ran under their byline with my documents attached.

hooks.description: I haven't spoken to my sibling since a row over who would pay for our mother's care home, and the last thing either of us said was something about money I wish I could take back.
The person who passed my unpublished investigation to a rival outlet still sends me messages, and I have never answered one.

voice.description: A Pakistani accent, a Punjabi and Urdu speaker. A man in his early thirties. Medium pitch, dry and even timbre, measured pace with brief pauses, flat and plain in manner, with clear consonants and little lift at the ends of sentences.
voice.reference_line: I check every figure twice before a story goes anywhere near print, because a wrong number outlives the apology.
